questions.stem: What is Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), and how is converting spoken audio into text different from identifying speakers or generating speech?
options: ASR changes audio into words by first matching each speaker against a stored voice identity, which supplies the transcription. Speaker recognition provides the actual word sequence, while speech synthesis reverses the audio format without requiring written text.

ASR converts spoken language in audio into a text transcript. Speaker identification or diarization concerns who spoke or when voices changed; text-to-speech instead starts with written text and generates audio, rather than recognizing spoken words.

ASR transcribes speech by assigning a new text label whenever the speaker changes. Speaker identification converts the remaining sounds into words, while speech synthesis analyzes the recording to decide which voice originally produced it.

ASR recognizes spoken content by locating fixed keyword boundaries and copying stored phrases into a transcript. Speaker identification determines each word's pronunciation, while speech synthesis produces the same recording with a different speaker label.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) turns spoken audio into written words. For example, a meeting assistant might write “Call Mia today” after hearing that phrase. Speaker identification asks whose voice it is, and diarization marks when different people speak; neither automatically supplies the words. Text-to-speech works in the other direction by creating audio from text. These technologies can work together, but a transcript answers what was said, not necessarily who said it.

questions.stem: How do sampling rate, audio waveforms, and log-Mel spectrograms represent speech for ASR, and why is correct audio resampling important?
options: Audio samples represent amplitude over time, while log-Mel features summarize sound energy across frequencies and time. The sample rate controls compression rather than timing, so the same stored samples can be relabeled without altering speech duration.

Audio sample rate specifies how often sound amplitude is measured, and a log-Mel spectrogram summarizes frequency energy over time. To change rates, engineers can update waveform metadata without changing sample values, because pitch remains unaffected.

A waveform stores audio amplitude over time, while log-Mel features represent time-frequency energy. Resampling means dropping or adding samples until the length looks suitable, without considering the signal's frequency content or anti-aliasing requirements.

Waveforms store sampled sound amplitudes, with sample rate giving samples each second. Log-Mel spectrograms summarize frequency-band energy across short time frames. Proper resampling changes sample values to match the rate expected by the model.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A waveform is a sequence of sound-amplitude measurements. Its sample rate says how many measurements occur per second; at 16 kHz, one second contains 16,000 samples. A log-Mel spectrogram summarizes how sound energy changes across frequency bands and short time windows. Some ASR models accept waveforms directly, while others use spectrogram features. Imagine receiving a radio recording at the wrong sample rate: simply changing its label can distort timing and pitch. Resample the signal properly instead.
questions.figure:
02 · VISUAL LESSON

Sample the waveform, then organize sound into frequency bands

Waveform: amplitude across time

A sample rate of 16,000 Hz means 16,000 amplitude samples per second.

Log-Mel spectrogram: time × frequency

Short-time frequency energy helps show changing speech sounds.

1 second × 16,000 samples/second = 16,000 waveform samples. Changing a file's rate label is NOT resampling.

Correct resampling changes the samples to the intended rate. Merely telling the recognizer a different sample rate can alter apparent pitch and timing.

questions.stem: How do acoustic evidence and language context help an ASR model recognize similar-sounding phrases, and why do noise, accents, and reverberation cause mistakes?
options: ASR combines evidence about speech sounds with learned language patterns to choose plausible word sequences. Similar phrases may need surrounding context, while noise, accents, and reverberation can distort cues that separate one word from another.

ASR uses acoustic evidence to propose words and language context to select a plausible sentence, even when that sentence conflicts with clearly spoken sounds. Noise and accents mainly lower confidence without changing which words are recognized.

ASR identifies speech sounds frame by frame, then uses language context to replace unfamiliar pronunciations with common words before decoding. This prevents noise-related errors but sacrifices unusual names, even when the acoustic evidence is strong.

ASR combines audio and language context by always selecting the most grammatically likely phrase, even when sound evidence favors another transcript. Noise and accents affect only the model's confidence score rather than the recognized words themselves.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Speech sounds do not always identify a unique phrase on their own. “Ice cream” and “I scream” can sound similar, but the surrounding sentence helps. An ASR system uses acoustic evidence along with language patterns learned during training or decoding. Noise may hide consonants, reverberation can blur sound boundaries, and unfamiliar accents can change the pronunciation patterns the model expects. A useful model combines context with what was actually heard instead of letting a likely sentence overrule clear audio.

questions.stem: How do CTC, transducer (RNN-T), and attention encoder–decoder ASR models differ in alignment, decoding, and support for streaming speech?
options: CTC requires a known token for every audio frame during training and learns no blank symbols. RNN-T ignores previously generated text, while attention encoder–decoder models must output full transcripts at once without predicting words sequentially.

CTC learns frame-to-token scores and removes blanks, but treats repeated adjacent symbols as separate characters. RNN-T relies only on earlier text rather than sound, while attention models align to fixed frame positions supplied by annotators.

CTC scores audio frames and collapses blanks and repeats without aligned labels. RNN-T uses acoustic features and prior tokens for streaming; attention encoder–decoders predict text from context and need adaptations for streaming.

CTC, RNN-T, and attention-based ASR all assign one fixed text token to each input frame. Their main difference is whether punctuation is produced automatically; all three can stream continuously without any restrictions on future audio context.
questions.explanation: Explanation: CTC predicts token scores across audio frames and uses a blank symbol plus a collapse rule to recover text without explicit frame-level labels. RNN-T also learns alignments but conditions predictions on both audio and previously produced tokens, making it useful for streaming designs. Attention encoder–decoder models learn how to use acoustic context while generating text; some depend on more of the utterance unless adapted. For live captions, architecture choices affect when words become available and whether earlier partial text changes.
questions.figure:
04 · VISUAL LESSON

Three ASR families, three ways to align sound and words

CTC

Frame token probabilities, with blank and repeated-token collapse.

Transducer (RNN-T)

Combines acoustic state and previous text; streaming-capable variants.

Attention encoder–decoder

Predicts tokens from learned acoustic context; some versions use full utterances.

All three model families convert acoustic evidence to text, but alignment and decoding differ. Whether a model streams depends on its complete architecture, not its name alone.

questions.stem: How can Python turn frame-level ASR token scores into a transcript using greedy CTC decoding, and why must repeated symbols and blanks be handled in the right order?
options: Greedy CTC decoding chooses the highest-scoring symbol at each frame, removes blanks immediately, then collapses repeated symbols. This preserves intended double letters because blanks cannot separate equal symbols once the blank frames have already disappeared.

Greedy CTC decoding selects the highest-scoring symbol at each frame, collapses consecutive identical symbols, then removes blanks. A blank between identical letters keeps them separate, so paths like l–blank–l can correctly produce two letters.

Greedy CTC decoding sums token scores over the entire utterance before choosing the strongest letters in order. Blanks are interpreted as word boundaries, and consecutive repeats remain because each frame was recorded separately.

Greedy CTC decoding keeps every repeated token because consecutive sound frames describe different parts of the word. It removes blanks after converting tokens to text, then chooses the most probable transcript using a mandatory language model.
questions.explanation: Explanation: CTC models may emit the same letter over several neighboring audio frames, plus special blank frames. Greedy decoding picks the top-scoring symbol for each frame, merges consecutive identical symbols, then removes blanks. The order matters: l, blank, l becomes two l's because the blank separates them. The runnable example uses artificial frame scores that decode to “hello,” not real microphone audio. A production recognizer first generates token scores with a trained acoustic model; more advanced decoding may consider alternative sequences.
questions.figure:
05 · VISUAL LESSON

CTC: collapse repeated frame symbols, then remove blanks

Framewise best tokens

Collapse consecutive repeats

[h, h, _, e, l, _, l, o] → [h, _, e, l, _, l, o] → hello
Python · CTC greedy decoding 10 lines · standard library only
vocab = ["_", "h", "e", "l", "o"]
path = [1, 1, 0, 2, 3, 0, 3, 4]
scores = [[int(i == k) for k in range(5)] for i in path]
best = [max(range(5), key=lambda k: row[k]) for row in scores]
out, previous = [], None
for token in best:
    if token != previous and token != 0:
        out.append(vocab[token])
    previous = token
print("".join(out))  # hello
Output: hello. The scores are synthetic one-hot examples, not output from a trained ASR model. For real speech, obtain logits from an acoustic model first.

A blank between two identical letters allows both to survive. If blanks are removed first, the intended “ll” can incorrectly become one “l”.

questions.stem: How is Word Error Rate (WER) calculated from substitutions, deletions, and insertions, and why can a low overall WER hide important ASR failures?
options: WER counts substituted, deleted, and inserted words but divides by the predicted transcript's length. A low average error rate reliably shows that every accent and specialty term is recognized accurately, making separate subgroup evaluation unnecessary.

WER adds substitutions, deletions, and insertions then divides by all words across both transcripts. Lower WER means fewer errors, so a strong overall score can replace checks for speaker variation, domain terms, and rare mistakes.

WER divides the count of wrong words by the number of audio frames, with each missing word scored as one frame error. Overall WER alone measures how consistently the system recognizes accents, names, and critical terms.

WER adds substitutions, deletions, and insertions, then divides by the number of reference words. Lower is better, but an overall score can hide errors involving accents, noise, unfamiliar languages, names, or critical spoken commands.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Word Error Rate compares the transcript with the correct reference words. A substitution replaces a word, a deletion omits one, and an insertion adds an extra one. Divide their total by the number of reference words. In the delivery instruction “send two boxes at noon,” a transcript saying “send three boxes noon please” has one of each error: 3/5 = 60% WER. Even a low overall WER can hide serious mistakes with names, medications, accents, or specific speaker groups.

questions.stem: How should production ASR systems address noisy audio, multiple speakers, multilingual speech, streaming latency, privacy, and leakage-resistant evaluation?
options: Production ASR should filter noisy samples and select its best preprocessing on the final test speakers, then report a single overall WER. Speaker diarization and data retention can be decided after launch because they do not affect transcription quality.

Production ASR can prioritize fast average decoding and train with repeated recordings from the same speakers in both training and testing. Multilingual variation is handled by changing only the transcript language label; privacy depends mainly on microphone quality.

Production ASR should test noise, accents, languages, and multiple speakers; measure streaming tail latency and subgroup WER; isolate held-out speakers and recordings; and protect audio with informed consent, access controls, retention limits, and ongoing drift monitoring.

Production ASR should reduce latency by recognizing each microphone chunk without considering neighboring sound, then combine independent transcripts. A low overall WER ensures fair subgroup accuracy, while storing all recordings indefinitely improves later retraining reliability.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A live call-captioning service needs more than accurate words in a clean demo. It may use voice activity detection for speech segments, diarization when speaker labels matter, and streaming decoding to reduce delays. Check noisy calls, languages, accents, and overlapping voices separately; measure tail latency, not just averages. Keep speakers and related recordings isolated between training and final evaluation to avoid leakage. Obtain appropriate consent and restrict audio access and retention. Monitor errors and changes in microphone conditions after deployment.
questions.figure:
07 · VISUAL LESSON

Stream safely, then audit errors across real conditions

Low-latency streaming path

Speech detection and chunking can reduce unnecessary processing; partial text may change.

Reliability and safety checks

Use independent test speakers and measure latency, subgroup WER, privacy, and drift.

Speaker diarization, language identification, and retention controls may be added as needed. A low average WER alone does not prove reliable service for every user.
